description: Regen

Aceraceae. Acer saccharin. Hard maple subgenus (lobes but no teeth). Leaves opposite, but lobes have no serrations; middle lobe is squarish. Buds have imbricate (overlapping) scales, are brown and sharp-pointed (red maple has blunt red buds). Bark light and can get flaky. Fruit a double samara w wings not diverging (nearly parallel). Mature in fall. In mts at higher elevations, cove forests, 30-40 gallons of sap = 1 gallon of maple syrup. Differ from Black maple--BM has black bark and wings on double samara diverge.

description: Sugar Maples are deciduous trees which flower in April and May. They can grow 25 to 35 meters tall, and occasionally up to 45 meters. The leaves can be up to 20 cm long, with 5 lobes. The basal lobes are small while the upper lobes are large with deep notches. The fruit is called a samara and is a winged seed, allowing the seeds to be distributed by the wind. The bark tends to be shaggy in older individuals. Sugar maples have famously and historically been used to produce the maple syrup that Canada and Northern New England are known for. They are found in much of northeastern North America, and are ecologically important to many hardwood forests. The Rosy Maple moth lays its eggs on the undersides of Sugar Maple leaves and the young that hatch feed on the leaves.

description: The sugar maples are starting to drop fruit. To be technical about it, these are schizocarps ("schizo" is splitting and "carp" for fruit) of samaras (one seeded, winged fruit). To be less technical about it, helicopters! The red and silver maples dropped fruit in the spring, so there's not much to confuse these with, and they have their own distinctive look, anyway. They are smaller than silver maple fruit, browner than both species, and have the fattest seeds of the three. These fruit could have stayed in the tree a little longer, but between thunderstorms, hail, and seed-eating birds, it can be hard to hang on. Notice the trio of damaged fruit. We may not think of these dry fruit as tasty, but goldfinches and likely cardinals are happy to pull out and eat the succulent seeds.

description:
We planted this sugar maple today to celebrate dad Tom Jett’s birthday, number 74 yo today. 
Courtney drove to White Oak nursery today, and bought 54 native (all but 2 fragrant viburnum) trees and shrubs. The first new plants that we have purchased and arrived here at the property. 
We planted this sugar maple in the west hedge row, about 3 feet from the boundary line. 
Really shouldn’t have planted it today, because it is so wet, our property is the wettest it has ever been, the pond the most full it has ever been, and our property on the west hedgerow is submerged in water. Still, we decided to plant a sugar maple anyway, today, to celebrate dad’s birthday. We hope it lives. We planted it with some added sticks and leaves at the bottom of the hole, and then about a gallon of compost that we made over the winter, mixed around the plant between it and the wet clay soil. When Caleb dug the hole, it filled most of the way back up with water! That area has never been wet before. Caleb said he looked it up and this is an especially wet spring right now.

description:
I am not much practiced in telling the various Maples apart. This fine tree interested me enough to try to identify it though. It is growing in an interesting way in a picturesque spot where it can be easily located over long term time (the next few centuries ahead). 

Its trunk is now about 28 centimeters (11 inches) in diameter a meter or so above the ground, and the whole tree leans over a small creek with its roots somewhat undercut and exposed. They all spread out into the streambank and are large and somewhat moss-covered. The tree as a whole seems stable, but sort of suspended above the water. A nice quiet place for me to sit. 

In addition to the native and beautiful Sugar Maple, I believe there may also be Black Maple and perhaps an occasional Norway Maple in this valley. This is in the eastern upper reaches of the Buffalo Creek watershed, on the Allegheny Plateau surrounded by old sheep and cattle farms and hills covered with mixed mesophytic deciduous second growth forest. Elevation around 342 meters ( feet).

description:
80' is the listed average amount, but this tree was roughly 30 feet tall.  Crown rounded, dense.  Leaves 5", opposite, with deep, long-pointed, few-toothed lobes; multicolored in fall (red, orange, yellow).  Bark smooth and gray-brown, becoming deeply furrowed, gray.  Key 1 1/4"; wings at 60 degree angle.  Habitat: Valleys, mtns, forests, field edges.  Range: Entire region, ex. coastal plain.

Facts came from the National Audubon Society Field Guide to the Mid-Atlantic States.

Species interaction:  I did not directly witness any specific species interact with this Sugar maple, but I know that their is human interaction with them elsewhere around Jennings Environmental Education Center because they are tapped to harvest sap in able to make maple syrup.  I have done some research, and found that real maple syrup is rich in antioxidants  and has a good amount of manganese in it as well.  Also, even though a hole is poked into the tree, the tree can easily recover from it if it is done  correctly.
